title: The endocrine system: hormones and glands
content:
The hormonal system is built from glands — organs that release chemicals — and the hormones they release. A hormone is a chemical messenger released directly into the bloodstream. Hormones are carried everywhere the blood flows, but each one produces a response only in particular places: its target organs. Hormones match with receptors on (or inside) their target cells, in the same lock-and-key way enzymes match their substrates: a hormone that fits nothing else finds the cells it can act on.

The glands to know

  • The pancreas releases insulin (and another hormone, glucagon) to control the level of glucose in the blood — the subject of the next two pages, and the one you must know in detail.
  • The adrenal glands release adrenaline, the hormone that prepares the body for sudden action: it raises the heart rate and breathing rate and readies the muscles for “fight or flight”.
  • Extension: the pituitary gland in the brain is the “master gland”, releasing hormones that control other glands, and the thyroid gland in the neck releases thyroxine, which sets the pace of body processes such as the rate of respiration. Labelling these as extension means they deepen your understanding but are not the CCEA focus of this chapter.

A common misconception: hormones are not the same as enzymes, even though both are chemicals that the body produces. Enzymes (lesson 1.2) are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions inside cells and are not used up. Hormones are messengers: they carry instructions from one part of the body to another and are broken down once their message has been delivered.

Practice

Insulin is released by one gland and acts on the liver and muscles. Use this example to explain what a target organ is.

Show the answer

Insulin is released by the pancreas and travels in the bloodstream, which carries it all around the body. A target organ is a part of the body whose cells have the matching receptors for a particular hormone, so only those cells respond to it. For insulin, the liver and the muscles are target organs: their cells take up glucose when insulin arrives, while cells without the matching receptors are unaffected.

title: Insulin and blood glucose control
content:
Every cell in your body runs on glucose — it is the fuel for respiration, the process that releases energy. The blood carries a steady supply of it. But the level of glucose in the blood must be kept within a narrow range. If it climbs too high, glucose damages organs and blood vessels over time; if it falls too low, the brain, which cannot store fuel, stops working properly. Eating a meal floods the blood with glucose; sleeping through the night drains it. Something must correct both changes, and that something is the pancreas.

Correcting a rise: insulin at work

  1. You eat a meal containing carbohydrate, which is digested into glucose that is absorbed into the blood. The blood glucose level rises.
  2. The pancreas detects the rise and releases the hormone insulin into the bloodstream.
  3. Insulin travels to its target organs. It makes body cells take up glucose from the blood more quickly, and it makes the liver (and muscles) convert the surplus glucose into glycogen, an insoluble storage carbohydrate that is packed away in the liver.
  4. As glucose leaves the blood and is stored, the blood glucose level falls back to the normal range, and the pancreas slows its release of insulin.

This pattern — a change away from normal triggering a correction that restores the normal level — is called negative feedback. It is the body’s standard method of keeping conditions constant, and the pupil reflex works the same way.

Extension. The correction for a fall in blood glucose is a second hormone from the pancreas: glucagon makes the liver convert stored glycogen back into glucose and release it into the blood, raising the level back to normal. Insulin and glucagon work against each other as a pair of controls.

Worked example: ordering the events

The question. Put these events in order after a person eats a slice of bread: insulin released by the pancreas; glucose level falls back to normal; glucose absorbed into the blood; glycogen stored in the liver.

Step 1. Start with the stimulus — the food must be digested and the glucose absorbed into the blood before anything else can happen.

Step 2. The rise in glucose is detected by the pancreas, which responds by releasing insulin.

Step 3. Insulin’s effects come next: cells take up glucose and the liver stores the surplus as glycogen.

Step 4. The final state is the result of those effects: the glucose level falls back to normal. The correct order is therefore glucose absorbed into the blood → insulin released by the pancreas → glycogen stored in the liver → glucose level falls back to normal.

Practice

Explain why the pancreas is described as both a receptor and an endocrine gland in blood glucose control.

Show the answer

Receptors detect changes: cells in the pancreas monitor the level of glucose in the blood passing through them, so the pancreas acts as the receptor for this control system. An endocrine gland is an organ that releases a hormone into the blood, and the pancreas does exactly that — it releases insulin (and glucagon) in response to what it detects. It therefore fills two roles in the same chain: it detects the stimulus and it releases the chemical that brings about the correction.

title: Diabetes: when blood glucose control fails
content:
Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot control its blood glucose level properly. Glucose stays high in the blood after a meal — a state called hyperglycaemia — and the excess glucose spills over into the urine, taking water with it. This explains the classic symptoms: passing large amounts of urine and feeling constantly thirsty (the body loses water), tiredness (cells cannot take up glucose properly for respiration) and weight loss (the body starts breaking down fat and protein for fuel instead).

There are two main types, with different causes and different treatments.

Type 1 diabetes

In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas does not produce enough (or any) insulin. The control system is missing its correcting hormone entirely. Type 1 usually appears in childhood or the teenage years, and it is not caused by lifestyle. Because no insulin is produced, it cannot be treated with diet alone: people with Type 1 diabetes inject insulin (using a syringe or an insulin pump), match the dose to their food and activity, and check their blood glucose regularly. Injected insulin works because it is delivered into the blood or fat tissue below the skin, from where it reaches the bloodstream — insulin cannot be swallowed as a tablet because, being a protein, it would be digested in the stomach like any other protein.

Type 2 diabetes

In Type 2 diabetes the pancreas still produces insulin, but the body’s cells no longer respond properly to it. The message is sent, but the target organs have stopped listening. Type 2 usually appears later in life, and it is strongly linked with obesity — a recognised risk factor. Treatment starts with lifestyle changes: a balanced, carbohydrate-controlled diet, regular exercise and weight loss, which often restore the cells’ response. Medicines that help the body use insulin, or extra insulin itself, are used if lifestyle changes are not enough.

Practice

A doctor finds that a patient’s blood contains plenty of insulin, but his blood glucose is still too high after meals. Which type of diabetes is most likely? Justify your answer.

Show the answer

Type 2 diabetes. The pancreas is producing insulin (it is present in the blood), which rules out Type 1, where the problem is that insulin is not produced. The problem must therefore be that the body’s cells are not responding to the insulin that is there — the defining fault of Type 2 — so glucose is not being taken up and the level stays high.

title: Measuring reaction time (practical)
content:
Reaction time is how long a person takes to respond to a stimulus. It is a direct measure of the nervous system at work: the stimulus starts an impulse, the message travels along the reflex arc or to the brain, and the effector muscle responds — and everything you have learned in this chapter happens inside that fraction of a second. Because the response is involuntary, measuring reaction time needs a method that does not rely on the person judging their own timing.

The ruler-drop method

Work in pairs. One person holds a metre ruler vertically, with the 0 cm mark at the bottom, between the thumb and first finger of the other person, who holds their fingers about 5 cm apart at the 0 mark. Without warning, the first person releases the ruler, and the second person catches it as fast as they can by closing their fingers. The distance the ruler dropped before the catch is read from the mark level with the top of the catcher’s fingers.

The distance is then converted to a reaction time using a prepared table of values (because the ruler accelerates as it falls, the conversion is not a simple proportion). The whole test is repeated several times and a mean is calculated, because any single measurement is affected by chance variation — the catcher may be distracted, or anticipating the drop.

Making the investigation fair

  • Independent variable: the factor you deliberately change — for example, testing the effect of a distraction (a partner asking questions), of caffeine, or of which hand is used.
  • Dependent variable: the distance the ruler falls (converted to reaction time).
  • Control variables: everything kept the same so only the independent variable can explain a difference: the same person as catcher, the same hand (unless hand is the independent variable), the same ruler, the same gap between the fingers, the same height of release, and warnings eliminated (drops must be unpredictable).

Worked example: calculating a mean

The question. A student’s three trials give reaction times of 0.19 s, 0.21 s and 0.26 s. Calculate the mean reaction time, and suggest why the trials differ.

Step 1. Add the values: 0.19 + 0.21 + 0.26 = 0.66 s.

Step 2. Divide by the number of trials: 0.66 ÷ 3 = 0.22 s.

Step 3. Check the reasonableness of the result: 0.22 s lies between the fastest (0.19 s) and slowest (0.26 s) trials, as a mean must. The mean reaction time is 0.22 s.

Step 4. The trials differ because a human is being measured, not a machine: attention wanders, the catcher may anticipate some drops (catching early) or be distracted (catching late). Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of these chance variations — a single trial could not fairly represent the person’s true reaction time.

Practice

Explain why the ruler must be dropped without any warning or pattern of timing, and why several measurements are taken.

Show the answer

If the catcher can predict when the ruler will be dropped, they can prepare — even start closing their fingers before the stimulus occurs — so the measurement would no longer reflect true reaction time. Unpredictable drops keep the test a genuine response to a stimulus. Several measurements are taken because each single trial includes chance variation (momentary distraction, luck); calculating a mean from repeats gives a value that fairly represents the person’s reaction time and reduces the influence of any one unusual result.

title: Chapter review
content:
This chapter followed a single chain through two control systems: stimulus → receptor → co-ordinator → effector → response. In the nervous system, the co-ordinator is the central nervous system — the brain for conscious and some automatic responses, the spinal cord for reflexes. Messages travel as electrical impulses along sensory, relay and motor neurones, crossing synapses as chemicals. Reflexes trade conscious control for speed, protecting the body before the brain is even aware of the danger. The eye supplied two worked examples: the pupil reflex, adjusting how much light enters, and accommodation, changing the shape of the lens to focus near and far. The hormonal system handles the slower, longer-lasting jobs. Its messengers are hormones released by glands into the blood, acting only on their target organs — and its central example was the pancreas releasing insulin to correct rises in blood glucose through negative feedback. When that control fails, the result is diabetes: Type 1 where insulin is not produced, Type 2 where cells no longer respond to it. The practical closed the chapter by putting your own nervous system on a stopwatch.

Key terms to be able to define

stimulus · receptor · co-ordinator · effector · response · central nervous system · neurone · sensory, relay and motor neurone · synapse · reflex action · reflex arc · voluntary action · pupil · accommodation · hormone · gland · target organ · insulin · glycogen · negative feedback · diabetes · reaction time

A common misconception: hormones do not travel along nerves, and nerve impulses do not travel in the blood. The two control systems use different routes entirely — electrical impulses along neurones for the nervous system, chemicals carried in the bloodstream for the hormonal system. A question that mixes the two routes has mixed the two systems.

Exam-style practice

Question 1. A person touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away.

(a) Put these in order: impulse passes along a motor neurone; pain receptor in the skin is stimulated; muscle in the arm contracts; impulse passes along a sensory neurone; impulse crosses a synapse onto a relay neurone in the spinal cord.

(b) Explain why the person’s hand moves away before they feel the pain.

Question 2. The blood glucose level of a student was measured every 30 minutes from lunchtime.

(a) Describe the role of insulin in returning the blood glucose level to normal after lunch.

(b) The student’s blood glucose remained high, although insulin was present in the blood. Name the type of diabetes this suggests, and give one difference between its treatment and the treatment of the other main type.

Show the answers

1(a). Pain receptor in the skin is stimulated → impulse passes along a sensory neurone → impulse crosses a synapse onto a relay neurone in the spinal cord → impulse passes along a motor neurone → muscle in the arm contracts.

1(b). The reflex arc is completed in the spinal cord: the relay neurone passes the message straight to the motor neurone, so the muscle contracts without the conscious brain being involved. A separate message travels on to the brain, but because it has further to travel and the reflex has already produced the response, the movement happens first and the feeling of pain arrives a moment later.

2(a). The rise in blood glucose after lunch is detected by the pancreas, which releases insulin into the blood. Insulin travels to its target organs: body cells take up glucose from the blood, and the liver and muscles convert the surplus into glycogen and store it. As glucose leaves the blood, the level falls back to normal — negative feedback — and the pancreas reduces its output of insulin.

2(b). Type 2 diabetes: insulin is present, so the pancreas is still producing it, which means the cells must be failing to respond to it. Type 2 is treated first with diet and exercise changes, whereas Type 1 — where insulin is not produced — must be treated with insulin injections, matched to meals and monitored blood glucose. (These questions are written in the style of CCEA examination questions but are original practice material for this course, not past examination questions.)

Where to go next
